Towards a Global Pact for the Environment: Some
Legal Reflections
Lydia Kriki
I. INTRODUCTION
Law-making regarding the environment has been in process for almost ﬁfty
years; as widely agreed, the 1972 Stockholm Conference triggered a global
regulatory
process.
Not
only
did
it
end
up producing
the
celebrated
Stockholm Declaration,1 which may be considered the founding act of environ-
mental law, but it also was followed by many other important instruments: the
1972 World Heritage Convention2 and the 1973 Convention on International
Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora3 are some examples.
Consequently, it is a ﬁeld that could be considered to be newly built; it was
created to respond to modern needs and recent developments. But, even if these
laws are truly necessary, humanity should primarily understand another import-
ant reality: that there are other laws that are equally considerable. They are the
fundamental laws of nature, which have been violated for almost one hundred
years in the name of progress—or, in fact, in the name of proﬁt. And, despite the
deﬁnitely striking disproportionate place of humankind on Earth (only 0.01
percent of the total biomass of the planet),4 its destructive impact is indisputable.
Humans, who have proven to be extremely efﬁcient in exploiting natural re-
sources, have culled and, in some cases, eradicated, wild mammals for food or
pleasure on virtually all continents.5 Since the rise of the human civilization, 83
percent of wild mammals have been lost, which is a tremendous disaster for the
balance of the ecosystems.

This tragedy has triggered many law-making efforts for the protection of the
environment. Until today, these efforts were fragmentary and unilateral; most
of the treaties regulate certain sectors of the environmental challenge, such as
climate change, desertiﬁcation, marine protection, or air pollution. Since this
mentality has proven not to be very successful, a new initiative rose in 2007;
the French legal think tank Le Club des Juristes—a gathering of the most
prominent jurists of the world— independently started a series of debates
and legal propositions on the most controversial questions of the law (‘un
lieu inde´pendant de de´bats et de propositions juridiques’).6 Among all of the
subjects that the Club des Juristes has discussed, environmental concerns have
an outstanding position. The Club des Juristes called for the nations to act on
behalf of the environment7 and proposed a legal tool with a universal ap-
proach; it was the ﬁrst time that an instrument considering the environment
in globo was introduced.
This instrument was the Global Pact for the Environment (Global Pact), which
served as the ﬂagship of the French think tank. Not only was it advocated by the
French government and by Pre´sident de la Re´publique Emmanuel Macron
during the launching summit (sommet de lancement) back in 2017 on the side-
lines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York,8 but it was
also seized by the European Commission, which sought a mandate from member
states to negotiate the Global Pact.9 The Commission characterized the proced-
ures leading to the adoption of the Global Pact as ‘a fresh opportunity to con-
solidate key environmental principles in one international text,’10 and it
reminded the community that the European Union has some of the most
advanced and comprehensive environmental policies in the world. Ultimately,
on 10 May 2018, the UNGA adopted, by an overwhelming majority, a resolution
that paved the way for the negotiations on a Global Pact for the Environment, as
will examined later in this article.

II. NORMATIVITY: AN OPTION FOR ENVIRONMENTAL LAW
1. Interplay of Hard and Soft Law
For many years, international environmental law followed a legal paradox com-
pared to general international law. While the legal production of soft law texts
was galloping along, the respective production of binding documents was
merely limping. The oxymoron of this situation would be obvious if someone
bore in mind the need for international environmental law to be ﬂexible and
resilient. On the other hand, this trend also created another ‘kind of normativ-
ity’— that is, numerous statements, declarations, and resolutions with a legal
value that are widely accepted as being debatable.11
The origin of international normativity, of course, is the notorious Article 38
of the Statute of the International Court of Justice (ICJ Statute), which mentions
the three formal sources of international law: the manifestations of the rights and
obligations of states, on which the International Court of Justice (ICJ) can base
its decisions to settle the disputes submitted to it.12 As stated, the article in
question is ‘de´claratoire [du droit international ge´ne´ral] en matie`re de sources.’13
And, despite the fact that members of the academic community state that the
article has lacunae or that it sometimes may be deemed to be ‘truncated’14 or
‘outmoded,’ Article 38 has mostly served its purpose of providing the court with
a basis for its decisions.15 The three sources listed in the ICJ Statute are (i)
international conventions; (ii) international custom, as evidence of a general
practice accepted as law; and (iii) the general principles of law. As one can
easily detect, it is a strict classiﬁcation applying speciﬁc criteria—once a legal
document does not fulﬁll them, it cannot be considered as a source of interna-
tional law.
A. ‘Environmental’ Normativity
Through the years, the need for adaptability in the ﬁeld of environmental law has
led to the application of the so-called ‘ﬂexible standards.’ Thus, along with

TOWARDS A GLOBAL PACT FOR THE ENVIRONMENT: SOME LEGAL REFLECTIONS
3
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/yielaw/advance-article-abstract/doi/10.1093/yiel/yvz061/5652059 by guest on 23 March 2020

international conventions, environmental law has adopted a wide range of acts
that were not legally binding, as they were missing the traditional characteristics
of international law emanating from one of the formal sources of Article 38. But
the fact that states have accepted soft law principles not only has negative as-
pects. It also facilitates, in fact, the formation of international customary norms.
A customary norm is composed of two distinct elements: the ‘material’ or ‘ob-
jective’ element, represented by state practice, and the ‘psychological’ or ‘sub-
jective’ element—that is, opinio juris.16 The existence of these two elements is a
strong indication that the state has conducted an act because it has the conviction
of being compulsory.
With respect to ‘soft’ instruments, it has often been stated that the cumulative
enunciation of the same guideline by numerous non-binding texts helps to ex-
press the opinio juris of the world community.17 This observation, although
different in character, should be viewed in light of the one made in 1986 by
the ICJ with regard to several important resolutions adopted by the UNGA: ‘The
effect of consent to the text of such resolutions . . . may be understood as an
acceptance of the validity of the rule or set of rules declared by the resolution by
themselves.’18 One should certainly not systematically go this far in interpreting
the frequent repetition of ‘soft’ rules in different kinds of texts. However, it is
likely that, through this notion, a new ‘opinio juris’ has emerged among nations
thanks to the frequent reiteration of certain identical principles. Many customary
principles have been recognized in regard to international environmental law.
The ICJ has identiﬁed the customary status of the no-harm principle in its ad-
visory opinion in Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons19 and has
acknowledged the obligation to conduct an environmental impact assessment as
customary in Pulp Mills on the River Uruguay case.20
Several fundamental principles are also contained in many soft law texts. For
example, it is widely known that the principle of sustainability was ﬁrst included
in the Rio Declaration in 1992,21 and the right to an ecologically sound envir-
onment was ﬁrst mentioned in the Stockholm Declaration.22 On the ﬂip side of
the coin, these principles, incorporated in such texts, lack legal force, and their
status remains simply declaratory. The purpose of the Global Pact that was
launched in 2017 is to codify these principles in a legally binding instrument.23

YEARBOOK OF INTERNATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL LAW
4

The drafters of the Global Pact strongly declared their intention to launch an
instrument of ‘hard’ law. It has been argued and widely felt among scholars that,
since these principles have been crystallized over a very long period, the time
has arrived for them to be vested with binding force.
On the other hand, one should not overlook the indisputable fact that the
function of an instrument in the hands of a state deﬁnes its normative perform-
ance; the outcome it produces weighs far more than its form or title. Numerous
examples in international law include texts that have been launched as ‘treaties’
or ‘agreements’ but which have not had the normative echo that the signing
states had anticipated. Most of the multilateral environmental agreements
(MEAs) that the international society has adopted so far have proven to have
comprised soft obligations at their core, despite the fact that they belong to the
so-called ‘hard law.’24 This fact is a direct consequence of the process by which
these agreements are set in force—namely, that MEAs are concluded as frame-
work agreements, which provide the skeleton of the regulations that will be
‘ﬂeshed out’ later on, according to the states’ readiness and the level of scientiﬁc
certainty in the ﬁeld.25
Since these agreements have to accommodate different and, many times,
competing interests, it is more convenient to have a form that will allow the
text to evolve and unfold, shifting to the next level of normativity when the
conditions mature. This scenario is evidence that it is not the title of the legal
instrument but, rather its use that is essential; it is possible for treaties to have a
‘soft belly’ and for declarations or resolutions to have a signiﬁcant normative
halo around them,26 enough for a change in state practice to be noted. The form
is never a barrier, as has been proven many times in international law and
sometimes even by the ICJ itself.27
(i) Environmental concerns: redeﬁning the landscape of the sources
Since, as we underscored, environmental law mainly consists of soft law elem-
ents, it is worth referring to its law-making process. In this process, the UNGA
holds a central position; it has played a catalytic role in the launching of various
global regulatory frameworks and has intervened in the direction of new legal
solutions. Most recently, the UNGA voted for the adoption of the Global Pact
through its Resolution 72/277.28 According to the resolution’s text, the UNGA

TOWARDS A GLOBAL PACT FOR THE ENVIRONMENT: SOME LEGAL REFLECTIONS

has decided to establish an ad hoc open-ended working group to consider a
technical and evidence-based report that identiﬁes and assesses possible gaps
in international environmental law and environment-related instruments with a
view to strengthening their implementation in order to facilitate the adoption of
the Global Pact for the Environment.29
The working group held its ﬁrst meeting on 14–18 January 2019, its second
meeting on 18–20 March, and its last meting on 20–2 May 2019, all in Kenya,
Nairobi. In the ﬁrst session, many conversations were held on the gaps in inter-
national environmental law and on the different options to ﬁll these gaps; the
proposition of Global Pact was not the main focus of this discussion. It was in
the second session where the Global Pact was discussed more intensively,
wherein, the conversation shifted from a previous reﬂection focused primarily
on the report of the United Nations (UN) Secretary-General to a broader and
constructive discussion on possible options to improve the effectiveness of inter-
national environmental law. Finally, the last session led to a unanimous, but
controversial, outcome, and the intervention that resulted was of minor import-
ance. As the summary of the session indicated, the working group concluded the
decision to recommend to UNGA to ‘forward the recommendations to UNEA
[United Nations Environment Assembly] for its consideration, and to prepare . . .
a political declaration for a UN high-level meeting . . . with a view to strengthen-
ing the implementation of IEL, and international environmental governance in
line with paragraph 88 of the Future We Want.’30
In other words, it resorted to the solution of a political statement, instead of a
more acute choice, and urged the UNGA to proceed to another soft law docu-
ment, instead of what many members of the international society expected and
wished for.31 Many scholars were also disappointed by the outcome since they
had anticipated a more appropriate reaction of the ad hoc group to the formed
reality. As this ﬁnal decision has serious implications, the question remains: is it
possible to make an effective use of a political declaration that could be adopted
by the United Nations Environment Assembly (UNEA) in 2021 and by a UNGA
resolution in 2022?

The UNEA is the world’s highest-level decision-making body on the envir-
onment, addressing the critical environmental challenges facing the world
today.32 It is also the main organ for producing soft law instruments that call
for action on the ﬁeld of the environment. It has adopted many resolutions
responding to the main environmental problems of our world, such as desertiﬁ-
cation,33 sustainable development,34 oceans and seas,35 and the preservation of
wildlife.36 It serves as the plenary organ of UNEP,37 which has progressively
developed a large number of environmental law texts, according to its mandate
to ‘promote international co-operation in the ﬁeld of the environment and to
recommend, as appropriate, policies to this end.’38 UNEP has also played a
leading role in the promotion of many regional conventions and, surprisingly,
has also evolved into a standing structure for negotiating draft resolutions sent to
the UNGA. At the UNGA, UNEP’s exhortations have been either passed with no
change or expressly referred to in its resolutions. It has the competence for
drawing up the reports presenting the annual ﬁndings on the global status of
nature, and it gives the main directions by suggesting policies and strategies.
Through these actions, the central issues of environmental concern are charted,
and the road to a possible solution is paved.
Of course, these texts, as UNGA resolutions, are not strictly regulative. Their
language is hortatory, inspirational, and indeterminate, if not simply declaratory.
But their importance cannot be downgraded. They are texts that incorporate the
intention of states to act,39 and this intention is a material element without which
an agreement would be considered as ‘sans porte´e juridique.’40 The difference,
in other words, lies in the effect that the states aim for the instrument to have. If
the parties do not will the international agreement to bring obligations and
rights, then the text is rendered void of legal effect. If, on the other hand, the
states negotiate the agreement bearing in mind that they will be bound—at any
level—by it, it is this volition that equips the text with a regulative force. It is
really impressive that this volition is obvious in the cases where the states invoke
vividly the agreements and the commitments emanating from them, even if the

TOWARDS A GLOBAL PACT FOR THE ENVIRONMENT: SOME LEGAL REFLECTIONS
7
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/yielaw/advance-article-abstract/doi/10.1093/yiel/yvz061/5652059 by guest on 23 March 2020

regimes established by them are not complete and if they evolve gradually. The
latter is a really common phenomenon in the ﬁeld of environmental law, where
the scientiﬁc data are ﬂowing with great frequency, and the experts’ estimations
may have changed during the course of the implementation of the agreement. As
Malgosia Fitzmaurice has noted, ‘[e]nvironmental law covers events which are
characterized by very speedy changes and by the need for prompt response to
environmental crises.’41
In these cases, the parties must try to make a basis for an evolving normative
process, by reaching a consensus even if the problem that the text regulates is
still changing. The states, in these cases, include in the provisions of the instru-
ments an amount of ‘calculated ambiguity’42 and a number of ‘mixed signals,’
which behave as ‘safety valves’ for the parties. In this way, the states can adapt
their reactions depending on their economic, political, and strategic choices and
follow their own pace, waiting for the normativity to harden.
As a result, it becomes self-evident that the nature of these legal texts appears
to be permissive, but what must be stressed is that states have chosen to make it
permissive. There are not norms of various degrees of persuasiveness;43 it is
generally accepted that the hardness or softness of a law does not affect its
normative character.44 It is the duty of the states to handle these instruments
in a certain way in order for the various results to be achieved—from a heavily
regulative framework to a simply transitory stage to the normative threshold,
with the expectation that it will transform to a ‘requirement.’
(ii) Advantages of a binding legal text
The progressive crystallization of soft law norms is an indicator of their author-
ity, which should now be formally recognized. A treaty enclosing this kind of
law would be the greatest recognition, and this treaty may be the proposed
Global Pact. Through the Global Pact, a transposition of these principles into
legal obligations would be achieved—thus, international environmental law
would gain legal certainty and legibility. At this point, what needs to be high-
lighted is that there is a huge range of treaties. On the one side of the normative
continuum, there are the treaties that, having a hard law character, are the
framework conventions or protocols. On the other end of the spectrum, there
are the non-legally binding instruments that are mostly politically acceptable by
states. Their content matters more than their form, and sovereign states prefer
this ‘latitude’ and ﬂexibility in their implementation. There is a whole panorama

YEARBOOK OF INTERNATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL LAW
8
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/yielaw/advance-article-abstract/doi/10.1093/yiel/yvz061/5652059 by guest on 23 March 2020

of normativity in the ﬁeld of environmental law, but the treaties that provide for
justiciable rights offer the most complete legal protection since they arm their
content with the possibility of judicial intervention.
And this is the most important result that the transposition of environmental
principles will achieve—namely, the fact that environmental law will become
justiciable. Since the fundamental principles of environmental protection will be
included in a treaty, it will be possible for them to be invoked before a judge. By
applying a binding Global Pact, domestic courts will have the possibility of
monitoring the application of environmental law through the compliance of
national laws to the Global Pact. Many states have included in their
Constitutions such legal principles,45 but the references are very limited.
Instead, an extensive catalogue of all of the ruling principles would be extremely
useful for the consolidation of the legal ediﬁce of environmental law. However,
the national judicial review of compliance with the Global Pact and its proced-
ures remain issues that are mainly national, which are delicate to deal with
within the pact itself given the diversity of the domestic legal systems.
International adjudication of environmental claims would likely improve
compliance, but enforcing compliance has been a sensitive matter, mostly be-
cause it involves the matter of the sovereignty of the states concerned. This has
led to the suggestion of creating new judicial institutions with compulsory jur-
isdiction over environmental disputes in order to facilitate the enforcement of
the right to a healthy environment and of states’ duty to take care of the envir-
onment. The Club des Juristes has expressed its approval of the creation of
speciﬁc new monitoring bodies for the effectiveness of international environ-
mental governance.46 It is widely known that the existing institutions cannot
achieve compliance since they lack the requisite power to penalize non-compli-
ant states. The administrative body that will monitor the implementation of the
Global Pact would be useful since many states may have the will to apply the
Global Pact, but they do not have the resources or the institutional capacity to do
so.47
In addition, for enhancing environmental governance, many scholars have
supported the idea of the establishment of an International Court for the
Environment, with a mandate similar to the European Court of Human Rights.
It is important to note that any efforts to promote such kind of institution should
not come at the expense of thoughts to strongly encourage or even require
parties to codify the Global Pact’s principles within domestic law, thereby

leveraging domestic legal systems to enforce a right to a healthy environment,
along with other principles commonly included in soft law instruments.
Allowing for domestic enforcement of the Global Pact’s provisions would
also emphasize the notion that the Global Pact aims to act as a treaty not only
among states but also between states and their citizens, having the ‘horizontal
effect’ of a human rights treaty.48 In addition, the provision for a right to a
healthy environment included in the Global Pact would encourage such an
interpretation.
(iii) The disadvantages of the paradigm shift
Pointing out that ‘it would not necessarily be advantageous to turn non-legally
binding principles into legally binding ones,’ Columbia law professor Susan
Biniaz argues that, while principles like the precautionary principle are useful
as considerations, they would create ‘confusion’ if converted into hard law.49
Others might approach such conversions more favourably but worry that incor-
porating strict commitments into the Global Pact might hurt its ability to attract
broad participation.50 I do not share these views since the time for the next step
has come, and this step would entail positive developments for environmental
governance.
III. TOWARDS A GLOBAL PACT FOR THE ENVIRONMENT
1. Why a Pact?
With respect to a high-level, environment-centred instrument, many efforts have
been made before: from the panegyric, grandiose declarations of Stockholm and
Rio, to the more spiritual, ethically oriented Earth Charter, the contributions in
the environmental ﬁeld, which have sought to safeguard the human habitat, are
numerous and impressive. They are characterized mainly by inspirational lan-
guage and formal wording,51 depicting not only universally accepted ideas but
also high expectations. Although they recognize the problems and urge for
action, the defect of all of these instruments is their legal nature; all of the
above are soft law examples, echoing widely accepted notions but limited in
the level of suggestions.

2. Goals of the Proposed Pact
The legal think tank Club des Juristes had three major goals in mind when it
started this initiative. First of all, the Global Pact was intended to ﬁll in the gaps
of the previous legal instruments that were unable to achieve integration in the
ﬁeld of environmental law. Second, it was also aimed at environmental protec-
tion through adjudication; it has already been largely known that the pact pro-
vides for a justiciable right—the right to the environment.68 Third, the Global
Pact was also something that was, in a sense, groundbreaking for international
law as it involved both state and non-state actors in the process of environmental
protection. It is an innovative approach, adopted also in two other draft com-
pacts: the Global Compact on Refugees69 and the Global Compact for Safe,
Orderly and Regular Migration.70 The participation of civil society in the con-
struction of the Global Pact is vivid and has had a major impact on the normative
character of the text. It has contributed to the transformation of the fundamental
principles into norms that can be adopted by private actors at the subnational
level.71 Of course, there are many things that must be done for an international
treaty to penetrate the sphere of private governance, but a Global Pact for the
Environment will begin the process.

(A) Cohesion of Environmental Law
During the past quarter century, international environmental law has proceeded in
a sector-speciﬁc approach that has led consequently to treaties that are well
tailored to address speciﬁc challenges72 but that are not appropriate to form a
cohesive ‘environmental code.’ This has happened, to some extent, because these
treaties entail an abundance of diverse technical norms that could not provide a
complete legal framework that is both integrated and self-contained. Moreover,
while this ‘piecemeal’ ad hoc approach has resulted sometimes in certain binding
commitments from member states, it has not provided for the ‘globally accepted
substantive human right to a good or clean and healthy environment,’ which the
Stockholm Declaration invoked back in 1972.73 Accordingly, the victims of the
various environmental harms have had to be resourceful, resorting to other rights
such as the right to health, food, water, and an adequate standard of living, in order
for a right to the environment to be implied.74
The proposed Global Pact promises to bring normative coherence to interna-
tional environmental law through the fact that it may be a binding instrument.75
The pact’s antecedents include, as mentioned, the Stockholm Declaration, the
Rio Declaration, the 1992 Agenda 21 (a mainly soft instrument that almost
became part of the developmental processes in most UN countries),76 and the
body of the Sustainable Development Goals, which did not have any binding
force, although they bore indicative value, presenting the international commu-
nity’s tendency regarding the solutions of a particular problem. In this way, the
Rio Declaration, for example, made clear the intention of states to integrate
environmental protection in their national policies. But, nowadays, merely de-
picting a major trend is no longer useful; states have to act in a particular way,
and this is possible only through a binding treaty. The Global Pact will incorp-
orate all of the regulations needed for a framework of environmental protection
and will bring legal uniformity. The provisions will now be enlisted in one text,
characterized by the same spirit and having universal force. The purpose of unity
will be served.

3. Towards a Uniform Interpretation
The second goal that the proposed Global Pact could serve seems to be the
uniformity of interpretation among the different kinds of law. The fragmentation
of international law has been a reality for many years. It is a reality with clearly
negative aspects since such fragmentation affects the systemic unity of the law
and the possibility for unhampered references to the jurisprudence. Except for
the ICJ, which is the ‘general competence’ court of international law, almost
every other judicial body has its own interpretation of the basic concepts of
international law. This is the pathology of international law; it does not indicate
the inherent resilience of international law to grapple with changing times and
challenges. Instead, it denotes inconsistency and partiality. It is a long-standing
malfunction caused by the uneven development of the various speciality ﬁelds;
human rights protection, investment arbitration, and environmental law are only
a few of the many examples.
During the course of years, different areas of law have been evolving inde-
pendently, responding to diverse needs emerging in the various points of time.
The phenomenon of the ‘compartmentalization’ of the law has appeared and has
continued to thrive through time.83 In this sense, public international law has
ended up being characterized by anarchy,84 which has had an impact even on the
judicial bodies of ‘general competence,’ such as the ICJ. Respectively, numer-
ous different fora were established to address sectoral matters: trade, develop-
ment assistance, oceans, investment protection, and human rights. But, on the
other hand, these partiality-centred institutions have been called upon increas-
ingly to address cross-cutting issues of general international law (for example,
extraterritoriality or reservations to treaties). And since they are challenged to
apply norms arising from different subject matter areas, it is easily understood
that this directly affects the interpretation of the law, as each legal ‘regime’
seeks to resolve any normative conﬂicts by favouring its own body of rules.
For example, this phenomenon was recently observed in the judgments of
many trade panels in the framework of the World Trade Organization (WTO)
system that came to a decision that was mostly pro-market. And, despite the fact
that the WTO itself has expressed the necessity for a dialogue between envir-
onment, energy, and trade,85 it is still debatable if the WTO is able to address
sensitive environmental issues. The most recent example was the ﬁndings of

The interrelationship between the different kinds of rules of international law is
governed by the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of the Treaties (VCLT).89
The VCLT, traditionally, is the most appropriate tool for ascertaining the rules
that govern a questionable relationship. The regulative ‘umbrella’ of the VCLT
addresses the problems arising between two or more treaties concerning the

rules of international law, including customary rules.92 Regardless of this set of
rules, however, the ICJ conﬁrmed in Case Concerning Military Activities in
Nicaragua that a rule can co-exist in a customary and treaty status at the
same time, and it was this decision that paved the way for the consolidation
of the status of custom.93

possible human right to a (decent, healthy, or sound) environment is to be es-
tablished, then it would have to be investigated if it is founded directly on the
architecture of the custom: is there enough state practice and opinio juris among
states for this to be deemed accurate?
Treaties are an important instrument for states to address possible environ-
mental problems;105 they also seem easier to interpret and implement. But what
should not be disregarded is that treaties traditionally are created through a
process of political negotiation leading to a state’s ﬁnal consent. Since, in the
course of such a process, some states are proven to be more inﬂuential than
others, treaties may become instruments for the powerful to assert their rights
against the powerless. The non-written sources of international may be proven to
be more equitable; changes in state practice may lead to a broader implemen-
tation of international law. Custom requires a continuous consistency that impels
every state, even the powerful ones, to act in a particular manner, even if it is
against its interests. In some way, a balance is achieved between state sover-
eignty and international community interests.
The jurisprudence of the ICJ has recognized in many cases the way in which
customary rules are linked to the concept of the territorial sovereignty of states
in the framework of environmental protection. The exercise of due diligence in
preventing signiﬁcant environmental harm is such a paradigm; the no harm
principle is one of the most well-known customary norms concerning environ-
mental protection. Thus, bearing in mind the principles of sovereign equality and
territorial sovereignty of states, the state of origin has the right to engage in
activities within and outside its own territory in order to avoid environmental
harms.106 But, when a state is obligated to take all of the necessary steps to
prevent environmental harm, must it also provide for a right to the environment,
thinking in a framework of state-centrism?107 If so, the environment would be
protected in a bidirectional way—for its own sake as well as for the sake of the
people living in it. Consequently, the question that arises is whether the envir-
onment itself could be deemed worthy of protection, irrespective of whether or
not the state’s sovereignty is injured.108
This contradiction was aptly depicted in the Corfu Channel case, where the
ICJ, of course, did not judge on environmental issues but, rather, grounded the

This is where the ﬁrst notion of the idea of Principle 21 of the Stockholm
Declaration, which addresses the limits of transboundary damage, can be de-
tected. The possible right to the environment itself may be deemed as an exten-
sion of this state obligation, as it expands the protection to the direction of right
to individuals.
Moreover, the need to provide for a human right to the environment may be
also drawn by other customary obligations, including the obligation to conduct
an environmental impact assessment, which was mentioned in the landmark ICJ
case Pulp Mills on the River Uruguay.110 By articulating this obligation for the
ﬁrst time, the Court stressed that a state’s economic development cannot be
lawfully exercised without regard for the detrimental impact on the environment
or human rights.111 Through this declaration, the ICJ called for the protection of
the natural habitat, but the purpose is twofold: safeguarding both this habitat as
well as the individuals surrounded by it.
The advisory opinion of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, although
it did not refer to it explicitly, invoked a human right to a healthy environment in
an innovative way. As a tool of interpretation, it also referred to custom as a
source of environmental obligations, underlining its overarching and regulative
role. Would it be the basis for establishing a human right to a healthy environ-
ment on the grounds of the different customary obligations imposed upon states?
The generality and ﬂexibility of international customary rules would be useful
for satisfying the needs of a large portion of the population worldwide; an
environment of a certain standard affects not only human life and health but
also dignity, equality, and education. The proposed Global Pact for the
Environment seems to contend the same notions; it attempts to embody custom-
ary principles in order to bolster a right to the environment and a duty for states
to behave in an environmentally sustainable way. It seems that the practice of
two international systems—one regional and one global—meet where human
needs are imperative; at the end of the day, law responds to reality and its order.

western modus vivendi had a destructive impact on our planet. The legal effect
of many of the legal texts adopted has been doubted many times in the past—
environmental law was indisputably the realm of the soft law attempts.
Consequently, the fact that the intentions of the Club des Juristes were chal-
lenged is not strange: many representatives of theory and practice thought the
proposed Global Pact would not be a binding text. But, the think tank sought to
contend that it could integrate the principles of customary law, the status of
which was conﬁrmed by both the academic circles and the jurisprudence many
times before. So, since the real question is not if the proposed Global Pact is
binding or not, but if it does integrate binding law, all the aforementioned
answer that the Global Pact, if at all materializes, will have binding force. In
fact, such a Global Pact could function as a framework convention, integrating
all of the axioms that have been for all these years the guide for the resolution of
any environmental dispute: they do already exist; the Global Pact will only offer
the binding scheme. It may also treat matters that have largely remained unad-
dressed or have ‘fallen between the cracks’ of international instruments, taking
the decisive step towards the future we desire and deserve, as the UN has
underlined before. As Rachel Carson described in her revolutionary work
Silent Spring:
[t]he history of life on Earth has been a history of interaction between living thing and
their surroundings. To a large extent, the physical form and the habits of the Earth’s
vegetation and its animal life have been molded by the environment. Considering the
whole span of earthly time, the opposite effect, in which life actually modiﬁes its
surroundings, has been relatively slight. Only within the moment of time represented
by the present century has one species—man—acquired signiﬁcant power to alter the
nature of his world.112
Let us hope that the proposed Global Pact, notwithstanding the outcome at the
end of the UNGA-mandated Nairobi Process on 22 May 2019,113 if it ever
materializes, could become the harbinger of hope for mankind to undo the
damage hitherto caused to the planet Earth. It may be an intervention with a
positive impact on us and on nature.
